Mortgage life or a level life benefit: chart the declining debt, premiums and payout destination

Four charts compare two hypothetical protection contracts over the same mortgage schedule, separating premium cash, conditional death benefits and the amount left after debt repayment.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two hypothetical first-term protection contracts against the same debt

Interactive planning lab

Mortgage remaining at the comparison date$295,184.58
Mortgage-life premiums paid through the horizon$7,200
Individual-policy premiums paid through the horizon$4,800

Hypothetical contracts, not insurance quotations. Both are assumed in force with any modeled death claim fully eligible and accepted. Mortgage-life limit equals the scheduled debt; an individual policy has the entered fixed benefit. Premiums are assumed flat for the comparison horizon; the mortgage-life premium stops after the month the debt is fully paid, while the individual premium continues. The same mortgage uses an unchanged nominal rate compounded semiannually, converted to an equivalent monthly rate, with month-end payments. No renewal-rate change, underwriting, policy exclusion, taxes, death probability, cash surrender value, investment alternative, portability decision or claims advice is modeled. Displayed claims are conditional amounts, not expected receipts.

The central idea

Compare what the contract covers and who receives an accepted claim, alongside its premium. A declining debt benefit and a level personal benefit are not the same promise.

01

Begin with the type of insurance, not just the word “mortgage”

FCAC’s mortgage-life rights guide distinguishes optional mortgage life insurance from mortgage default insurance. They address different events and should not be treated as interchangeable products.

This article compares two hypothetical death-benefit contracts: a mortgage-life limit tied to the remaining debt and an individual policy with an entered level benefit. It does not model default, disability, critical illness or unemployment coverage.

All insurance amounts and premiums are assumptions. The tool cannot determine whether a person qualifies, whether a claim will be accepted or which contract is suitable. The graphics assume both contracts remain in force and any illustrated death claim is fully eligible and accepted.

02

A debt-linked benefit can shrink as the mortgage is repaid

FCAC’s comparison of optional mortgage products describes mortgage-life benefits paid to the lender and decreasing with the mortgage balance. Its comparison with individual life insurance also identifies the different beneficiary and coverage structure.

The first chart uses those two structures as selected contract assumptions. The mortgage-life limit follows the scheduled debt after each payment. The individual policy’s entered benefit remains fixed throughout the chosen comparison period.

Neither curve is a probability-weighted payout. A level benefit above the debt does not mean that extra money will necessarily be received; an insured event and a valid claim are still required. A benefit below the debt leaves a funding gap in this deliberately limited comparison.

03

Use the same loan schedule under both insurance alternatives

The default begins with CAD 400,000 of mortgage principal, a 25-year amortization and a nominal 5% rate compounded semiannually. The model converts that quote to an equivalent monthly rate and calculates a level month-end payment.

The mortgage assumptions are identical under both insurance alternatives. Selecting a different premium does not change the loan’s interest rate or accelerate its repayment. Insurance premiums are separate cash expenses and are not treated as additional principal payments.

The comparison keeps the mortgage rate unchanged for the full displayed horizon. It therefore does not reproduce a real sequence of mortgage renewals. Fees, refinancing, extra payments, arrears and changes in the debt contract are excluded. A personal review should use the actual projected balance at the date being considered.

04

Follow the premium cash separately from the conditional benefit

The default mortgage-life premium is CAD 60 per month and the individual-policy premium is CAD 40. Over ten years, with the default mortgage still outstanding, those assumed cash commitments total CAD 7,200 and CAD 4,800.

The second chart accumulates the premiums as payments. They are not contributions to an investment account and do not create an accessible reserve. The illustration includes no savings component, surrender value or investment return.

Both premiums are assumed flat within the selected horizon. The mortgage-life premium stops after the month the debt reaches zero; the individual policy continues for the full comparison period. Those are model conventions. Actual renewal prices, expiry dates and termination conditions must come from the written policies.

05

Trace who receives an accepted claim and how cash is used

The third graphic assumes death immediately after the final scheduled mortgage payment shown in the selected horizon. For the mortgage-life example, the accepted benefit equals the remaining debt and is paid to the lender.

For the individual-policy example, the named beneficiary receives the fixed benefit and is assumed to choose mortgage repayment first. The chart separates the amount applied to debt from any residual. This use of the individual benefit is an illustration, not an automatic instruction imposed on the beneficiary.

If the entered individual benefit is too small, residual family cash is zero and the remaining debt is reported in the figure note. The waterfall shows benefit less outstanding mortgage. A negative endpoint means a debt-funding shortfall, not a negative insurance payout or a new loan.

06

Compare the actual promises before making a protection change

Price is one part of the comparison. Confirm the insured person, policy term, beneficiary, coverage limit, exclusions, evidence requirements and whether the contract continues when a mortgage is refinanced or moved. The calculator does not verify any of those terms.

FCAC’s rights guide calls for charges, express consent and cancellation information for applicable optional products, with a separate disclosure from a bank. Use that disclosure and the policy wording to ask questions about the actual contract, rather than treating this generic curve as a quote.

A family’s protection need may also include other debts, replacement income and near-term expenses. Conversely, other verified coverage or resources may already fund part of the need. This narrow two-contract illustration is not a complete insurance-needs analysis and does not recommend replacing or cancelling an existing policy.
